etymology: Greek Basileios, “kingly,” bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the fourth century, called Basil the Great.
biblical_def: Basil, called the Great, was bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia in the fourth century, the eldest of the three Cappadocian fathers who carried forward the Nicene cause after Athanasius. His chief doctrinal labour was the defence of the full deity of the Holy Ghost against those who would make the Spirit a creature; his treatise On the Holy Spirit set forth the Scriptural truth that to lie to the Holy Ghost is to lie not unto men, but unto God (Act 5:4), and that the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God (1Co 2:11). He confessed the one Godhead in three Persons, the Father, the Son, and the Comforter whom the Father sends in the Son’s name (Joh 14:26). Basil was also a tireless pastor, who built hospitals and houses for the poor and ordered the life of the church with rare diligence. The dictionary honours him as a great defender of the Trinity and of the Spirit’s deity, and a model of pastoral charity. Where the asceticism he fostered, and the honours later paid to such fathers, grew in time toward errors the Reformation had to correct, the rule remains the Scripture Basil himself defended; but his witness to the Godhead of the Holy Ghost stands among the church’s great treasures.
webster_summary: A fourth-century Cappadocian bishop, Basil the Great, defender of the deity of the Holy Spirit and a model of pastoral charity.
webster_full: BASIL OF CAESAREA, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, called Basil the Great.
He was the eldest of the three great Cappadocian fathers.
His treatise On the Holy Spirit defended the full deity of the Spirit.
He confessed the one Godhead in three Persons against the Arians.
He was a tireless pastor who built hospitals and houses for the poor.
scriptures: Act 5:4
Whiles it remained, was it not thine own? and after it was sold, was it not in thine own power? why hast thou conceived this thing in thine heart? thou hast not lied unto men, but unto God.
For what man knoweth the things of a man, save the spirit of man which is in him? even so the things of God knoweth no man, but the Spirit of God.
Now the Lord is that Spirit: and where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty.

corruption_summary: He defended the deity of the Holy Spirit against those who made the Spirit a creature, a truth the church still confesses.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Basil confronted was the denial of the Holy Spirit’s deity by the Pneumatomachi, who, granting the Son, would yet make the Spirit a creature. Against this Basil set the Scripture, where to lie to the Spirit is to lie to God, and the Spirit searches the deep things of God as none but God can. The dictionary honours his defence of the Spirit’s Godhead as a settled treasure of the church’s Trinitarian confession.

What is honourable in Basil is plain: his Trinitarian theology, his pastoral charity, his ordering of the church’s life. The dictionary honours these freely. Where the monastic discipline he fostered, and the veneration later generations paid to the memory of such fathers, drifted toward the excesses the Reformation corrected, the rule is the Scripture Basil himself defended. He is received as a faithful witness, not as an authority above the word; and his great gift to the church is the truth that the Comforter is very God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “kingly,” Basil names the Cappadocian defender of the Spirit’s deity.

usage: Like Basil, the church confesses the Holy Ghost to be very God, not a creature.
To lie unto the Holy Ghost is to lie not unto men, but unto God.
Honour the faithful father as a witness, never as an authority above the word.

etymology: Greek Gregorios, “watchful,” bishop of Nazianzus and briefly of Constantinople, called Gregory the Theologian.
biblical_def: Gregory of Nazianzus, the second of the three Cappadocian fathers, was so honoured for the depth and precision of his teaching on the Godhead that the church gave him the rare title of the Theologian. In his Five Theological Orations, delivered at Constantinople, he set forth the doctrine of the Trinity with a clearness that has fed the church ever since: one God in three Persons, equal in glory and majesty, the Father unbegotten, the Son begotten, and the Spirit of truth which proceedeth from the Father (Joh 15:26), all confessed in the baptismal name into which the nations are discipled (Mat 28:19). He stood for the full deity of the Spirit when many still wavered, and pressed home that the Word who was with God and was God (Joh 1:1) took our whole nature to redeem our whole nature. The dictionary honours Gregory the Theologian as one of the surest guides the early church gave to the doctrine of the Trinity. His benediction is the church’s own, that the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the communion of the Holy Ghost be with all the saints (2Co 13:14); and his precise confession of the three Persons in one God is a lasting bulwark against every form of the Arian and the modalist error.
webster_summary: A fourth-century Cappadocian father, Gregory the Theologian, master of the doctrine of the Trinity.
webster_full: GREGORY OF NAZIANZUS, bishop of Nazianzus, called Gregory the Theologian.
He was the second of the three great Cappadocian fathers.
His Five Theological Orations set forth the doctrine of the Trinity.
He defended the full deity of the Holy Spirit when many wavered.
He confessed the Word who took our whole nature to redeem it.
scriptures: But when the Comforter is come, whom I will send unto you from the Father, even the Spirit of truth, which proceedeth from the Father, he shall testify of me:
Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost:
Joh 1:1
In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.

corruption_summary: His precise confession of the three Persons in one God stands against both the Arian and the modalist error.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruptions Gregory confronted were Arianism, which denied the full deity of the Son and the Spirit, and modalism, which confounded the Persons. Against both he set forth the one God in three Persons, equal in glory, the Father, the Son, and the Spirit proceeding from the Father. The dictionary honours his Theological Orations as among the surest guides the early church ever gave to this doctrine.

What is honourable in Gregory is his Trinitarian precision and his defence of the Spirit’s deity. The dictionary receives this gladly. Like all the fathers, he is honoured as a faithful witness and not as an authority above Scripture; the doctrine he taught is true not because he taught it but because the word of God reveals it. His confession remains a lasting bulwark, and the church still prays his benediction of the grace, the love, and the communion of the Triune God.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “watchful,” Gregory of Nazianzus names the Cappadocian Theologian of the Trinity.

The Spirit of truth proceedeth from the Father, very God with the Father and the Son.

etymology: Greek Gregorios, “watchful,” bishop of Nyssa in Cappadocia, the youngest of the three Cappadocian fathers.
biblical_def: Gregory of Nyssa, younger brother of Basil and the third of the Cappadocian fathers, was a thinker of great subtlety who laboured for the Nicene faith. In his books Against Eunomius he defended the full deity of the Son against the bold Arianism of his day, and in his treatise On the Soul and the Resurrection he upheld the resurrection of the body and the life everlasting. For these labours the dictionary honours him. Yet Gregory also drank deeply of the speculations of Origen, and from that fountain he drew the error of the restoration of all things, teaching that in the end even the damned, and the devil himself, should be purged and brought home to God, so that hell should at last be emptied. This the dictionary names plainly as a corruption, contrary to the express word of the Lord, that the wicked shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal (Mat 25:46), and shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord (2Th 1:9). Gregory the defender of the Trinity is honoured; Gregory the universalist is refused. His error is a solemn warning that even a great mind, when it leans upon human speculation against the plain word, may overthrow the doctrine of eternal judgment that Christ Himself revealed.
webster_summary: A fourth-century Cappadocian father, defender of the Trinity, but marred by the Origenist error of universal restoration.
webster_full: GREGORY OF NYSSA, bishop of Nyssa, the youngest of the Cappadocian fathers.
He was the younger brother of Basil of Caesarea.
His books Against Eunomius defended the full deity of the Son.
His treatise On the Soul and the Resurrection upheld the life everlasting.
He fell into the Origenist error of the restoration of all things.
scriptures: And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal.
Who shall be punished with everlasting destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power;
Mar 9:48
Where their worm dieth not, and the fire is not quenched.
And the smoke of their torment ascendeth up for ever and ever: and they have no rest day nor night, who worship the beast and his image, and whosoever receiveth the mark of his name.
corruption_summary: His defence of the Trinity is honoured, but his Origenist doctrine of universal restoration is refused as contrary to the word of Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption to name in Gregory is the Origenist doctrine of the restoration of all things, the teaching that hell shall at last be emptied and even the devil purged and saved. This the dictionary refuses as a plain departure from Scripture. The Lord Jesus, who alone has the words of eternal life, declared that the wicked go away into everlasting punishment, where their worm dieth not and the fire is not quenched, and that the smoke of the torment of the impenitent ascends for ever and ever. The doctrine of eternal conscious punishment is no harsh invention of later ages but the express revelation of Christ, and no speculation of Origen or of Nyssa may set it aside.

What is honourable in Gregory is his defence of the deity of the Son against Eunomius and his witness to the resurrection of the body. The dictionary honours these. But his error is a solemn warning that even a great and subtle mind, when it builds upon human speculation against the plain word of God, may overthrow a doctrine the Lord Himself revealed. The church receives the fathers as witnesses, and weighs every one of them, the greatest not excepted, by the unerring rule of Scripture.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “watchful,” Gregory of Nyssa names the youngest Cappadocian, sound on the Trinity but Origenist on hell.

The wicked shall go away into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into life eternal.
The fathers are witnesses to be weighed by Scripture, the greatest of them not excepted.

etymology: Greek Kyrillos, “lordly” or “of the Lord,” bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, author of the Catechetical Lectures.
biblical_def: Cyril was bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century, and his Catechetical Lectures, delivered to those preparing for baptism, are among the most precious witnesses we have to how the early church instructed its converts. He led the candidates step by step through the articles of the faith, the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law, that they might come to baptism understanding what they professed. The dictionary honours this careful catechizing of converts, holding, as Cyril did, that the faith is to be taught and understood, not merely felt. Yet his lectures, especially the mystagogical addresses on the sacraments, show the sacramental theology of the church already drifting toward errors the Reformation had to correct: a heightened language about the bread and the cup, and a tendency to bind grace too tightly to the rite of baptism. Against such drift the dictionary holds the Lord’s own word, that it is the Spirit that quickeneth, the flesh profiteth nothing (Joh 6:63), and the Supper a remembrance that shews the Lord’s death till he come (1Co 11:24; 1Co 11:26). Cyril the catechist is honoured for his diligent teaching of the faith; the seeds of sacramental error in his lectures are weighed and refused by the rule of the word.
webster_summary: A fourth-century bishop of Jerusalem whose Catechetical Lectures model the instruction of converts, though tending to sacramental error.
webster_full: CYRIL OF JERUSALEM, bishop of Jerusalem in the fourth century.
His Catechetical Lectures instructed candidates preparing for baptism.
He led converts through the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law.
His mystagogical lectures show a drift toward heightened sacramental language.
He is honoured as a catechist while his sacramental errors are weighed.

For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come.
Joh 6:63

Tit 3:5

corruption_summary: His diligent catechizing is honoured, while the sacramental drift in his lectures is weighed and refused by the word.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Cyril is his catechizing, the patient instruction of converts in the creed, the Scriptures, and the moral law before they came to baptism. The dictionary honours this diligence, holding that the faith is to be taught and understood, and commending the church that does not receive members untaught.

The corruption to weigh is the sacramental drift his lectures display. Already in Cyril’s mystagogy the language about the bread and cup is heightened beyond the Scriptural memorial, and grace is bound too closely to the outward rite, sowing seeds that grew in later ages into the errors of transubstantiation and baptismal regeneration. Against this the dictionary holds that the Spirit quickeneth and the flesh profiteth nothing, that the Supper shews the Lord’s death as a remembrance, and that men are saved not by the bare washing but by the mercy of God and the renewing of the Holy Ghost. Cyril the catechist is received; the seeds of sacramental error in his lectures are refused.
roots_summary: From the Greek for “lordly,” Cyril of Jerusalem names the fourth-century bishop and catechist.
roots_lines: Cyril — Greek Kyrillos, “lordly” or “of the Lord.”

They witness to how the early church taught its converts.
They also show an early drift toward sacramental error.
usage: Like Cyril’s lectures, the church teaches its converts the faith before it receives them.
It is the Spirit that quickeneth; the flesh, and the bare rite, profiteth nothing.
The Supper is a remembrance that shews the Lord’s death till He come.

etymology: From the Syriac Aphrem, a fourth-century deacon and hymn-writer of the Syrian church, called the Harp of the Spirit.
biblical_def: Ephrem was a deacon of the Syrian church at Nisibis and Edessa in the fourth century, the greatest poet of the early church and a teacher who clothed sound doctrine in song. He saw that the heretics of his day, Bardaisan and the Arians, spread their errors in catchy hymns, and he answered them in kind, pouring the orthodox faith into verses that the people sang, so that the truth might dwell richly in them in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs (Col 3:16). For the sweetness and abundance of his hymnody he was called the Harp of the Spirit. The dictionary honours Ephrem as a master of teaching the church through holy song, and as a humble deacon who refused higher office to serve. Yet his poetry also poured forth some of the most exalted praises of the virgin Mary in all the early church, language that, however devout in intent, sowed seed for the later Marian errors of Rome and the East. Against this the dictionary holds that Mary herself rejoiced in God her Saviour (Luk 1:47), confessing her need of the one Mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1Ti 2:5). Ephrem the hymn-writer is honoured; the over-exalting of the creature, even the blessed mother, is refused.
webster_summary: A fourth-century Syrian deacon and hymn-writer, the Harp of the Spirit, who taught orthodoxy in song.
webster_full: EPHREM THE SYRIAN, a fourth-century deacon of the Syrian church.
He served at Nisibis and Edessa and refused higher office.
He answered the heretics’ hymns with hymns of the orthodox faith.
He is called the Harp of the Spirit for his sweet and abundant hymnody.
His exalted Marian praises sowed seed for later Marian errors.
scriptures: Col 3:16

Luk 1:47
And my spirit hath rejoiced in God my Saviour.
For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus;
Psa 40:3

corruption_summary: His teaching of orthodoxy in song is honoured, but his over-exalting of the virgin Mary is named as the seed of later error.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Ephrem is his holy hymnody. Seeing the heretics win the people with song, he answered them in song, and poured the orthodox faith into verses the church could sing, that the word of Christ might dwell in them richly. The dictionary honours this gift, by which sound doctrine was carried into the hearts of the simple, and the singing of the truth became a bulwark against error.

The corruption to name is the extravagance of his Marian praise. Ephrem’s poetry exalted the virgin in language that, however devout, went beyond the Scripture and sowed seed for the Marian devotion the Reformation had to call the church away from as a corruption of biblical Christology. The dictionary holds that Mary, blessed among women, herself rejoiced in God her Saviour and needed the one Mediator between God and men. The hymn-writer is honoured; the over-exalting of the creature, even the holiest of women, is refused, for the worship and the trust of the saints belong to God alone.
roots_summary: From the Syriac Aphrem, the name marks the fourth-century Harp of the Spirit and hymn-writer of the Syrian church.

His exalted Marian praises sowed seed for later error.
usage: Like Ephrem, the church may teach sound doctrine by holy and singable song.
Mary herself rejoiced in God her Saviour, owning her need of the one Mediator.
Worship and trust belong to God alone, never to the creature, however blessed.

etymology: From the city of Damascus, an eighth-century monk and theologian, the last of the great fathers of the Eastern church.
biblical_def: John of Damascus, a monk of the monastery of Saint Sabas near Jerusalem in the eighth century, was the last of the great fathers of the Eastern church and the gatherer of its theology into system. His chief work, the Fountain of Knowledge, with its third part, An Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith, summed up the teaching of the earlier fathers on the Trinity, the incarnation, and much besides, and became the textbook of Eastern theology for ages. For this labour of preservation the dictionary owes him a debt. Yet John is remembered above all as the great defender of the veneration of images in the iconoclast controversy, and here the dictionary must name his error plainly. He argued that because the Word was made flesh, the invisible God might now be pictured and the images honoured; but Scripture forbids the making of any graven image or likeness for worship (Exo 20:4), and warns that Israel saw no manner of similitude in the day the LORD spake out of the fire (Deu 4:15). God is a Spirit, and they that worship Him must worship Him in spirit and in truth (Joh 4:24). The dictionary honours John’s gathering of the fathers and his witness to the reality of the incarnation, while it names his defence of icon-veneration as a corruption of the second commandment, against which the Reformed church holds the regulative principle of worship.
webster_summary: An eighth-century Eastern father who systematized patristic theology but defended the veneration of images.
webster_full: JOHN OF DAMASCUS, an eighth-century monk and the last great Eastern father.
He was a monk of the monastery of Saint Sabas near Jerusalem.
His Fountain of Knowledge systematized the theology of the earlier fathers.
He was the great defender of image-veneration in the iconoclast controversy.
His defence of icons is named as a corruption of the second commandment.

Deu 4:15

Joh 4:24

corruption_summary: His gathering of patristic theology is honoured, but his defence of icon-veneration is named a corruption of the second commandment.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in John of Damascus is his preservation and ordering of the earlier fathers’ theology, and his witness to the reality of the incarnation against every shadow of docetism. The dictionary honours this labour, which carried the patristic inheritance forward to later ages.

The corruption to name is his defence of the veneration of images. John argued that because the Word was made flesh, the unseen God might be portrayed and the images honoured; but this overthrows the second commandment, which forbids the making of any likeness for worship, and the witness of Sinai, where Israel saw no similitude. God is a Spirit, to be worshipped in spirit and in truth, and the Reformed church, holding the regulative principle, admits into worship only what God has commanded. The dictionary honours John the systematizer while it refuses John the defender of icons, and names the veneration of images, however reverently intended, as idolatry forbidden by the word of God.
roots_summary: Named from Damascus, John marks the last great Eastern father, systematizer of theology and defender of icons.

usage: Like John of Damascus, a man may serve the church in learning yet err gravely in worship.

etymology: From the Latin Leo, “lion,” bishop of Rome in the fifth century, called Leo the Great.
biblical_def: Leo, surnamed the Great, was bishop of Rome in the fifth century, a man of weight and resolve who is remembered for two things above all. The first is his Tome, a letter on the person of Christ which was read at the Council of Chalcedon in the year four hundred and fifty-one and was received as a true statement of the faith: that in the one Person of the Son two natures, the divine and the human, are united without confusion or change, so that the Word was made flesh (Joh 1:14), and great is the mystery of godliness, God manifest in the flesh (1Ti 3:16). For this clear confession the dictionary honours Leo. The second thing is his vigorous building of the Roman claims, his pressing of the bishop of Rome’s primacy over all the churches as the heir of Peter. Here the dictionary parts from him. The rock on which Christ builds His church (Mat 16:18) is not the succession of Roman bishops but Christ Himself confessed, the chief corner stone, elect and precious (1Pe 2:6). The dictionary honours Leo’s Christology, which the church confesses with him at Chalcedon, while it names his papal pretensions as the seed of the very office the Reformation rejected on the warrant of Scripture.
webster_summary: A fifth-century bishop of Rome whose Tome shaped Chalcedon, but who advanced the papal claims the Reformation rejected.
webster_full: LEO THE GREAT, bishop of Rome in the fifth century.
His Tome on the person of Christ was received at the Council of Chalcedon.
It confessed two natures united in the one Person of the Son.
He vigorously advanced the primacy of the bishop of Rome.
His Christology is honoured; his papal pretensions are refused.
scriptures: Joh 1:14
And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us, (and we beheld his glory, the glory as of the only begotten of the Father,) full of grace and truth.

And without controversy great is the mystery of godliness: God was manifest in the flesh, justified in the Spirit, seen of angels, preached unto the Gentiles, believed on in the world, received up into glory.
And I say also unto thee, That thou art Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church; and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it.
Wherefore also it is contained in the scripture, Behold, I lay in Sion a chief corner stone, elect, precious: and he that believeth on him shall not be confounded.
corruption_summary: His Chalcedonian Christology is honoured, but his advancing of the papal primacy is named the seed of the office the Reformation rejected.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Leo is his Tome, the clear confession of the two natures in the one Person of Christ, which the Council of Chalcedon received as the faith of the church. The dictionary confesses this Christology with him: the Word made flesh, God manifest in the flesh, true God and true man united without confusion or change. On this Leo stood firm, and on this the church stands with him.

The corruption to name is his building of the papal claims. Leo pressed the primacy of the Roman bishop over all the churches as the heir of Peter, laying foundations on which the medieval papacy rose. But the rock on which Christ builds His church is Christ Himself confessed, the chief corner stone, not the line of Roman pontiffs; and the Scripture knows no universal bishop ruling the church of God. The dictionary honours Leo’s Christology while it refuses his papal pretension, naming it the seed of the office the Reformation, on the warrant of the word, called the church away from.

usage: Like Leo at Chalcedon, confess the Word made flesh, two natures in one Person.
The rock on which Christ builds His church is Christ confessed, not a line of pontiffs.
Honour a man’s true confession while refusing the error he joined to it.

etymology: From the Latin Vincentius, “conquering,” a fifth-century monk of the island monastery of Lérins in Gaul.
biblical_def: Vincent was a monk of the island monastery of Lérins off the coast of Gaul in the fifth century, remembered for his little book the Commonitory and for the rule of catholicity it set down. Against the novelties of the heretics he proposed a test: that we hold what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all, so that antiquity and consent might guard the church against every new invention. There is a true use in this. The faith was once delivered to the saints (Jud 1:3), and any gospel that contradicts the apostolic gospel, though an angel preach it, is accursed (Gal 1:8); novelty in doctrine is rightly suspect. The dictionary honours the Vincentian rule, soberly used, as a hedge against innovation. Yet Vincent meant his canon partly as a weapon against the Augustinian doctrines of sovereign grace, for he belonged to the semi-Pelagian party of Gaul that resisted Augustine’s teaching on predestination. And the rule itself, if exalted above Scripture, makes tradition the judge of the word rather than the word the judge of tradition. Against this the dictionary holds: to the law and to the testimony; if they speak not according to this word, there is no light in them (Isa 8:20). Antiquity and consent are servants of the Scripture, never its masters.
webster_summary: A fifth-century monk of Lérins whose canon of catholicity guards against novelty but was aimed against the doctrines of grace.
webster_full: VINCENT OF LERINS, a fifth-century monk of the monastery of Lérins in Gaul.
His Commonitory set down a rule of catholicity against the heretics.
The rule holds what has been believed everywhere, always, and by all.
He belonged to the semi-Pelagian party that resisted Augustine.
His canon is honoured against novelty but subordinated to Scripture.

corruption_summary: His canon of catholicity is useful against novelty, but he aimed it at the doctrines of grace and exalted tradition too near the word.
corruption_paragraphs: What is honourable in Vincent is the sober use of his canon. The faith was once delivered to the saints, and any new gospel is accursed; antiquity and the consent of the church are a real hedge against the novelties of heretics. The dictionary honours this use, and the Reformers themselves appealed to a chastened form of it, showing the Reformation to be no innovation but a recovery of the ancient and Scriptural faith.

The corruption to name is twofold. First, Vincent forged his canon partly as a weapon against Augustine’s doctrine of sovereign grace, for he stood with the semi-Pelagians of Gaul who resisted predestination; and a rule turned against the doctrines of grace is turned against the gospel itself. Second, the canon, if set above Scripture, makes tradition the judge of the word, when the word must be the judge of tradition. The dictionary holds the order plainly: to the law and to the testimony. Antiquity and consent are servants of the Scripture, useful in their place, but never its masters; and where they would silence the doctrines of grace, they are themselves to be silenced by the word.
roots_summary: From the Latin for “conquering,” Vincent of Lérins names the author of the canon of catholicity.

etymology: From the Latin Prosper, “favourable” or “prosperous,” a fifth-century lay theologian of Gaul and defender of Augustine.
biblical_def: Prosper of Aquitaine was a lay theologian of Gaul in the fifth century, the foremost defender of Augustine’s doctrine of grace in the generation after his death. When the monks of southern Gaul, the semi-Pelagians, rose against Augustine’s teaching on predestination and the bondage of the will, Prosper took up the pen for the doctrines of sovereign grace, contending that salvation is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy (Rom 9:16); that by grace are men saved through faith, and that not of themselves, it is the gift of God (Eph 2:8); and that no man can come to Christ except the Father draw him (Joh 6:44). The dictionary honours Prosper as a faithful champion of the very truths the Reformation afterward recovered: free and sovereign grace, election of God’s good pleasure, and the working of God in the believer both to will and to do of His good pleasure (Php 2:13). In his later years Prosper softened somewhat, giving more place to the universal call of the gospel; but he never abandoned the substance of Augustine’s doctrine. He stands as a witness that the doctrines of grace are no Reformation novelty, but the ancient confession of the church against every form of the Pelagian error.

corruption_summary: He defended the doctrines of grace against the semi-Pelagians, witnessing that sovereign grace is the ancient faith, not a novelty.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Prosper withstood was semi-Pelagianism, the error of the Gaulish monks who would make the first movement toward salvation the work of man’s own will, with grace coming in only to assist. Against this Prosper held the Augustinian and Scriptural truth that grace is sovereign and free, that salvation is not of him that willeth but of God that sheweth mercy, and that the Father must draw the sinner before he can come to Christ. The dictionary honours him as a faithful champion of the doctrines of grace.

What is honourable in Prosper is that he kept the faith of sovereign grace in an age that resisted it, and so handed it on. The dictionary marks that in his later years he gave more room to the universal call of the gospel, softening his earlier severity; yet he never abandoned the substance of Augustine’s doctrine. He stands as a clear witness that election and effectual grace are no invention of the Reformation but the ancient confession of the church, recovered, not created, by Luther and Calvin against the Pelagian error in its every form.

etymology: A Greek rendering, “house-lamp,” of the German surname Hüssgen, borne by the sixteenth-century Reformer of Basel.
biblical_def: Johannes Oecolampadius was the Reformer of Basel, a scholar of Greek and Hebrew and a master of the writings of the fathers, who turned from the learning of Erasmus’s circle to the gospel of the Reformation. He laboured to make the church of Basel a Reformed church, preaching that he was not ashamed of the gospel of Christ, for it is the power of God unto salvation to every one that believeth (Rom 1:16), and calling men to search the Scriptures, for in them is eternal life and they testify of Christ (Joh 5:39). His patristic learning served the Reformation well, for he showed from the fathers themselves that the Roman corruptions were later additions, and that the recovered gospel was the ancient faith. With Zwingli he held the Supper to be a remembrance that shews the Lord’s death till he come (1Co 11:26), and at the colloquy of Marburg he stood for the symbolic understanding of the sacrament against Luther’s bodily presence. The dictionary honours Oecolampadius as a faithful Reformer and biblical scholar, the very type of the patristic scholar whose learning the Reformation turned to the recovery of the gospel. Where the Reformed church refines the bare symbolic view into the doctrine of Christ’s spiritual presence received by faith, the substance of his protest against Rome’s corruption of the Supper stands.

corruption_summary: He turned his patristic learning to the recovery of the gospel, showing Rome’s corruptions to be later additions to the ancient faith.
corruption_paragraphs: The corruption Oecolampadius laboured against was the accumulated error of medieval Rome, which had buried the gospel of grace under the inventions of men. With the tools of Greek, Hebrew, and the fathers, he showed that the recovered gospel was the ancient faith and the Roman additions the novelties. The dictionary honours him as the very type of the patristic scholar whose learning served the Reformation’s return to the word, proving that to recover the fathers rightly read is to recover the gospel they confessed.

On the Lord’s Supper Oecolampadius held with Zwingli the symbolic view, against Rome’s transubstantiation and Luther’s bodily presence, contending that the sacrament shews the Lord’s death as a remembrance. The dictionary stands with his protest against Rome’s corruption of the Supper, while it refines the bare symbolic view into the fuller Reformed doctrine of Christ’s spiritual presence received by faith, which neither denies the sign nor confounds it with the thing signified. Oecolampadius the Reformer and scholar is honoured, and his recovery of the ancient gospel from the fathers is received with thanks.
